items.note: The footer signup field gets a 2px danger border and a red alert glyph with a one-line message that includes an example address. The ink Subscribe pill sits beside it on the cream rise-arc footer. The error is clear and stays in the system's language, like the reference's warm inline form states (09/11).

The error itself is well done: a danger border, a coral message and a white pill on the indigo footer band. But in all three samples the page ends in a bright white bottom bar under the navy night palette. The reference's night band (03) never breaks into a white slab.

The field spans the full width with a red border, the alert line sits under it, and a full-width ink pill follows, all on the cream footer. It reads at once and matches the reference phone's stacked, centred rhythm (04).

The form is replaced by a small white card with a tiny tick or crescent glyph and two lines of body text, at the very bottom of the page. It reads correctly but is timid, where the reference states outcomes boldly and the spec offers a sparkle toast or composition.

The same small inline confirmation card, in indigo on the indigo footer, so it barely separates from the band. Under it is the white bottom strip. It is legible, but it is a quiet line rather than a designed moment.
On the phone the confirmation is one small inline card at the bottom of a long scroll, with a tiny glyph. The reference would give a success outcome more presence than body-size text in a box.

Sample 1 builds a proper empty state: a crescent-shaded magnifier composition, an h4 title, a line and an ink pill on a cream panel. Sample 2 puts a lone pair of dots on a full yolk panel, and sample 3 uses a 24px ring. Both are far below the reference's spot-pictogram craft (07).

The night versions match the light ones. Sample 1's magnifier on indigo reads well. Sample 2's yolk panel carries just two dots, and sample 3's small ring glyph floats in an empty indigo panel. The structure (title, line, white pill) is right, but the art is thin.

The empty panels stack cleanly under the filter pills with full-width ink pills. The art is again a dot pair or a ring in 2 of 3 samples. In those same two samples the footer email input below collapses to a thin sliver.

The focused top-bar Home link gets a rounded blue ring in sample 1. In samples 2 and 3 it gets a flush square box that clips the area dot and the text edge. The reference's focus is a rounded ring offset from the pill (11).

In the night top bar, a yellow ring hugs the Home link, rounded in one sample and square and tight in the others. It is visible but cramped against the dot, unlike the reference's offset rounded ring.
Sample 3 rings the header's blue Subscribe pill with the reference's rounded 2px-offset ring. Samples 1 and 2 box the Home link, rounded in one and square in the other, flush against the text.

The post covers are strong. A megaphone, flag, branching path, moon, bowl, bell, envelope and bar chart are each built from crescent-shaded primitives, read without their titles, and are each their own drawing, close to the reference's pictograms (07). The hero cluster is the same orange disc, cloud and pill in all three samples. That is the disc-plus-cloud option the spec calls not the default, at about a fifth of the band's width.

The inline figures and related-post covers are good. The article header clusters are mostly generic: a hexagon with a pill, or a tilted card with a disc, that pictures nothing about the subject. Sample 2's disc-magnifier holding blocks is the exception. The reference's band art always reads as a scene (02).

In samples 1 and 3 the header cluster repeats the other article's hexagon-and-pill or card-and-disc unchanged, so the two articles look alike. Sample 2 puts the megaphone inside its disc, which is on subject. The covers below are well drawn and distinct.

The blue band art is a sun behind a cloud, a speech bubble with a disc, or a hexagon with a pill, each with sparkles in two sizes. Avatar discs carry crescent shading and initials. This is flat, confident work close to the reference's shape kit, with only sample 3's lead shape generic.

The hero text and art fade in once, confetti discs fade in, and one hero shape drifts slowly over 8s. A small zigzag glyph breathes on a 5.1s eased scale-and-rotate cycle, and the about vignette cards build in one by one. That is the reference's calm, sparse motion exactly as the spec describes it, with nothing bouncing.

findings.summary: In dark mode, every page ends in a bright white bottom bar under the navy page and indigo footer, which breaks the night palette. The spec causes it: the footer bottom bar is told to use `surface.inverse`, and that token is #ffffff at night.
findings.promptFix: Footer bottom bar: ink (`#2d2c2b`) by day and the night page navy (a step darker than the indigo footer band) at night, with on-dark text. Do not use `surface.inverse` for bands or bars, because it flips to white in dark mode. A dark page never ends in a light strip.
findings.specRule: Footer | Cream band with rise arc, link columns, a signup field + ink pill; `surface.inverse` bottom bar with round icon buttons

findings.summary: A newsletter signup's success is still a small inline card with a tiny glyph and body text at the bottom of the page. The spec's ink pill toast with a sparkle, or a small success composition, is unused, so the outcome is quiet where the reference states it confidently. This was named in rc.2 and rc.3 and is still open.

In 2 of 3 samples, the no-results empty state's only art is a lone pair of dots on a full yolk panel, or a 24px ring. The spec explicitly forbids a lone pair of dots and asks for a `size.art` composition or a `glyphLg` glyph. Sample 1's crescent-shaded magnifier shows the intended level.
On phones the footer email input collapses to a thin sliver above its full-width pill. This is an agent layout slip that has been seen since rc.2.
Top-bar text links still get a flush square focus box that clips the area dot in 2 of 3 samples. Pills get the reference's rounded ring offset 2px (11). This has been open since rc.2.

Band clusters are well drawn but rarely about their subject. The front-page hero is the same disc, cloud and pill in all three samples, and both articles' header bands reuse a generic hexagon-and-pill or card-and-disc, so the two articles look alike. The reference's band art reads as a scene for its topic (02). One sample's disc-magnifier and megaphone clusters show what is possible.
